title: Bad Genius (2017)

lines.narration: A sealed bag of pencils and erasers. Lynn gives her name, says the phone is not hers, offers her grades as proof.
In the dark an answer sheet fills itself in, row by row, until a name settles under the bubbles.
Then a file with her name on it. Certificates, a clipping, the record that makes her worth recruiting.
Lynn and her father sit before the administrator, trophies on the desk, a clipping naming her a national crossword champion.
Her father talks the record down to swimming, pushing trophies across. The director stops him - does Lynn want to come?
She answers for herself: the old school suits her better, and a year here costs almost a hundred and fifty thousand.
Sixty thousand a term, two terms. The number arrives handwritten beside her head: 120,000. She keeps itemising.
Her father's hand settles over hers as she finishes the sum - fares, lunch at thirty-five instead of twenty. Not worth it.
Then the figures vanish and the offer lands: what if she studies for free? Her father grins beside the trophies.
An enrolment form for 2557, and a nickname going onto the dotted line.
M.4. Three years gone, and the new school arrives as a queue of white uniforms climbing stone steps.
A stranger starts smoothing Lynn's hair at the backdrop. Three years here, she says, you have to look good. She is Grace.
Alone at a dark table, Grace repeats what people say about them: Lynn is clever, and Grace is stupid.
They spread a maths paper between them. A inside B, intersect C - Lynn walks it while Grace stares at the page.
A hand lands on Lynn's shoulder. Teach me how - and the astonishment is at Lynn, not the maths.
Grace names the terms: homework every evening, and she will be the first student Lynn ever teaches.
Back at the bare table: she only helped a friend study. She taught her nothing wrong. Did she?
Midterm. A hall of white uniforms, and Lynn at her desk with her head already down, writing.
Two seats over, Grace's page is blank - then a Venn diagram she knows, the same question off Lynn's pink worksheet.
Grace twists round and whispers back. Lynn answers alert, then her face folds. She knows what is being asked.
The proctor slouches and stifles a yawn. Lynn is the only head in the hall that comes up.
A metal pen, then something small in her fingers: answer letters pencilled down the side of a white eraser.
Lynn checks the front of the room. Grace's head snaps up, expectant. Lynn stays turned away.
She works her foot out of her shoe and drops the eraser inside. Then their eyes meet across the aisle.
The shoe is kicked out. It skids over the tiles and stops upright in the open, answers inside.
A student stands at the invigilator's desk. Under the rows a hand reaches into the shoe for the eraser.
Grace grins down at her sheet and writes. Lynn hands her paper in. Grace sits back with a lollipop.
In the corridor Grace hugs a report book and names the next thing: Pat's place. You have a swimsuit, right?
A robe stitched Patton Hotel Bangkok. Then night, a lit rooftop pool, and a boy surging through the spray: Pat.
Grace surfaces into it: smart people do not understand her, and stupid people still want a good grade.
Pat slaps water into the air and names a price: three thousand baht a term. Lynn lifts her head.
Three thousand each, he says, and five more of them want in. On a dark street, Lynn is still listening.
Thirteen exams, he totals it: two hundred and thirty-four thousand baht. Worth more, he says, than her cleverness.
At home, in the dark, she eases open her father's desk drawer and lifts out a sealed official document.
Under the lamp she sorts the papers and reads. The development fee was paid anyway - 120,000, scholarship or not.
Why this school, she asks from the piano. For chances he never had, he says. He is not like her mother.
He tips a pill into his hand and swallows it. Lynn drops her eyes. He sets the bottle down, smiling.
Alone, she works the same four fingerings until they stop being music. Four shapes, four answers on a multiple-choice sheet.
Paying a friend to teach you music, she will say later, is not illegal in any country.
In the music room she gives six students four chords and a right-hand position to read off her hands.
Three answers right, one wrong, repeated - and hold the scores down so nobody notices. The students stare back blank.
Final exam, 2/2557, half past eight to half past ten. Grace chews her pencil and waits for a hand.
Lynn plays the exam from her own living room while boy after boy reads the tapping hand and inks another row.
A bank book opens on deposits climbing into the hundreds of thousands. Then the house after dark, her father waiting.
On the school tower a banner unrolls: a portrait, congratulations on a scholarship. The school hangs up what it was handed.
The other top student gets his own title. Bank's portrait drains to grey over a school toilet block.
Inside a stall his face screws up and he doubles over. Then a card reading Bank goes on his shirt.
Backstage he divides the prize before they win it: five thousand baht, less the discount, half each. Lynn keeps her eyes shut.
His hair is a mess and she is fixing it, she says; he is on television now. He looks away, silent.
She lays a hand on him in the doorway and holds out a fist. He stares, then bumps it.
Teen Genius. Both of them at the contestant desk; pi comes back to twelve places and their school wins the week.
The director has news. One free Singapore scholarship, both of them sent to sit for it, and only one place per school.
Night. A headlight flares, a battered helmet goes on over earphones, and Bank walks the bike into a lit laundry.
Inside, a hand sets his certificate beside a memorial portrait. The shop is still working.
From a dark doorway he watches his mother crouched over the washing, one earphone in, her hands raw in the soap.
Leave it, he tells her, that hand will not heal. His textbook stays on the stool. He scrubs alone.
Lynn sits alone in near-darkness, then raises her head. The look hardens out of defeat into something decided.
A classmate stops him in the corridor: he cannot pass the paper, and offers three thousand baht. Bank walks away.
The hall exam. An earphone in Bank's ear, hundreds of desks ruled out in white tape. He watches the room fill.
The row settles into shading bubbles. Bank is sweating by the second half, his pencil stalled at thirty-nine and forty.
A student asks the proctor about question forty. There are two versions of the paper, and it asks which one you got.
Lynn's hand goes to her mouth. Her cover reads set one; Bank's forty has a filled bubble rubbed out.
Her code carries one set of answers; the hall is sitting two. She checks behind her and drives the pencil on.
Under the green lamp Bank reports what Lynn's hands have been doing. A second invigilator comes to the desk.
Past the lamp, a grid of bowed heads. He folds his arms, says he will see to it, and looks past Bank.
So the answers go out as finger taps. A hand drums the desk; a boy taps and writes at once.
A second header lands on a desk: set two. The fingers splay and drum a different rhythm.
Lynn sweats, left hand tapping while the right one writes. Then the invigilator steps out and heads come up.
Outside, a phone fills with the group chat. Pat counts the takings while Grace braids Lynn's hair. It has spread.
A grey-haired teacher in a tie passes the steps. The speakers call a student to the office. Grace stands up.
The teacher already has his informant. Bank told the school the exam had leaked, and that two different papers went out.
Lynn and Bank stand side by side, eyes down, while the teacher works a stack of answer sheets for the match.
Then it breaks. Lynn pushes past the doorframe and out; a boy in the glass door looks after her.
Through the office glass: the director, Lynn at the blinds, her father beside her. They have evidence she sat a friend's exam.
For the money, she says. A classmate paid her three thousand baht to sit it. Her father's head comes round.
She is not the only one making money here, Lynn says: two million baht, and they call it a fee.
Her father begs for her term. The condition: her scholarship is cut, and Singapore with it.
She never cheated, Lynn says. The marks were hers, and Bank deserves the place. The director looks up, stricken.
Her father keeps his eyes down and leaves with Bank. Bank's head stays lowered, Lynn's back in front of him.
A dark room, a glass of water sweating, Bank still answering. Find the evidence, he says, and she cheated.
A passbook tilts open to Lynn's name. Nobody earns three thousand baht that way, her father says across the table.
He unbuttons the shirt as he talks: he does not want it any more. She stays home and repays the money.
Lynn sits by a barred window in her uniform. Her head drops and her face comes apart.
Lynn has stopped taking the work. Grace sits down opposite and sells harder.
Lynn answers flat: they can manage two semesters without her. Nothing agreed.
Another table. Pat's father drains the wine; Lynn laughs along.
A Boston brochure slides across: go with Pat, tutor him into a school his grades can't reach.
The condition is STIC — one exam, sat the same day worldwide.
Six hundred thousand baht to go. Lynn says nothing, and takes the envelope.
A wall of hotel clocks. NEW YORK. Her face tightens, then opens.
Her eyes find SYDNEY, hours ahead. Sit the paper there and the answers reach Bangkok first.
A red pin goes down on Australia. Behind the glass, a print shop.
Lynn lays it out: their own scores, plus fees from other students, split after costs.
She can hold half the answers in a break. The other half needs one person, who will refuse.
Bank hauls the basket off his scooter: one more delivery, exam at eight tomorrow.
A parked car has been watching. A door opens; Bank stares straight back.
CCTV, 19:53. Men rush him and drag him down beside the pickup.
He comes round in rubbish, one eye swollen shut, a speck on a landfill.
He falls, gets up, walks on. His scholarship exam starts without him.
Then he stops looking for a way out and howls in the mud.
At school it is sold from a stage: spotlight, microphone, STIC logo.
Out in the rows the paying customers are already slumped.
Her method: a phone taped under a sink, answers sent out in the breaks.
Into the room with it: a barcode printed down a 2B pencil.
Bar thickness carries the answer, thickest to thinnest — A, B, C, D.
Bank sits in a dim back room, a bruise under his eye.
Daylight. Lynn walks into the laundry.
Bank's answer: cheating means somebody loses. Lynn says they are the losers already.
His life cheats him anyway, she says, and slides a card across his ledger.
He looks past her, refusing. Then he takes it — the no had a price.
Bank steps out of the dark of the print works. He is in.
Step one, Lynn says: she and Bank sit the exam in Sydney.
Then the drills, section by section; the clothes change, the run repeats.
Lynn calls time and Bank runs. The whole trip must fit one break.
Seven and a half million on a phone calculator, then a bag of notes.
Getting answers out: a phone taped inside a cistern lid, thumbs typing.
Pat and Grace grin as the answers land. Bank sits apart, head down.
The interview room again — this time Pat in the chair, crying into both hands.
It slips out at Lynn's back: the men at that gate were Pat's. Bank missed his exam because Pat paid for it.
Pat's voice goes up. Bank hears all of it, jaw set.
Bank comes over the desk. Lynn screams; they go down by the green wall.
Bank drives Pat into the door — Pat turns it round, gripping his shirt.
Lynn and Grace stand helpless while Bank's shouting breaks into crying.
Lynn holds Bank's look, then she is gone, and Grace is left with him.
A lit overpass. Lynn alone at the rail, hand over her mouth.
Bank comes up the ramp and stops dead, breathing hard.
Bank's answer is not no. He finishes it — she put him in that landfill, and he wants paying.
Their faces inches apart over the city lights. Two figures with a flight to catch.
Sydney, the day before. Head down, Bank tells her he is sorry.
He has never been abroad, he says. From tomorrow he can go anywhere in the world.
Then nothing. Two small figures at a railing, bags at their feet - the last quiet hour they get.
Exam morning. Bank stops chewing: the diner television has broken into a STIC bulletin on tighter monitoring.
At the centre an official briefs them. Watches come off; they go in carrying nothing.
Bank carries a bundled jacket into the men's toilet. Two doors shut, one each.
In the dark a panel comes away. A bagged phone, taped under a tray, ends up on Lynn's lap.
Bank's face appears in a gap in the partition. Both reach through.
The invigilator walks out. 8:29:58.
Her hand runs the grid - question 17, the clock at 8:51, bubbles to twenty-six, ahead of the paper so the answers can leave first.
Bangkok, still dark. In a shuttered print house a whiteboard maps the sections, the timings, the phones. Grace turns to Pat; the message goes.
At the break two phones come out of plastic wrap, Bank's first, then Lynn's, and answer strings start filling the chat.
Then the thread stops being answers. Bank wants another million. Lynn reads it in her stall, Pat in his.
He pounds the laundry bench and gives them five minutes to transfer, then turns on a worker behind the table.
He prices it out: the first million was the fee, the second is for the beating. Pat's disbelief sets into a scowl.
Pat sends back a transfer slip - everything in the account now, the rest when the answers come. Bangkok pays.
Barcodes map onto answers, 1A to 5C. A hand hits the button and the press starts.
Black pencils heap onto the steel bed, barcode strip peeled off. The mark on the pencil is the answer, printed while the exam runs.
Section 3, grid-in: sixteen questions, twenty minutes. She works the algebra and prints digits into the boxes.
In a locked cubicle Bank peels the phone out of a sanitary-pad wrapper and types BCADB, DCDAC, BDABC. Outside, Lynn listens.
Two men in suits come in; someone has reported how long he has been gone. His head snaps up, then back to the values.
The phone goes into the bowl and the flush carries it away. Outside, a proctor tilts his face up at the door.
In the corridor a grey-haired man jabs a finger at Bank, then grabs a fistful of his jacket. Lynn watches from the doorway.
Her face crumples and holds. Then she turns and walks back down the hall, because the exam is still running without him.
At the water cooler a hand dips into her boot, tears a wrapper, lifts the cup. She walks off, hands behind her back.
Section 4: thirty questions, thirty-five minutes. The pencil reaches thirty, and there is nothing left to carry it out on.
So she shuts her eyes, and the rows on her paper - A A D, C D B, B C A - become the piano she learned on.
The clock behind her reads 10:42. The code she built to sell answers is now the only place she can keep them.
The last section is an essay on a speech - nothing in it reduces to four letters.
Her own fingers go between her lips. She is not sick; she is making herself sick.
She buckles until the whole row is watching, and asks to be let home.
Leave now and her score is cancelled, the proctor tells her. She goes anyway, walked out in tears.
Bag on her shoulder she hurries down the corridor. A suited man rushes past: somebody has started looking.
She climbs the stairs while a suited man crosses the lobby, phone at his ear, telling someone he cannot see her.
In the station she sends a coded line about a speech transcript. In Bangkok the alert lands on a phone on cardboard.
She drops to her knees on the station floor and hammers out another block.
Grace types the phrase into search and Nelson Mandela speech transcripts fill the screen. The code opens.
Answer slips go into the rank of motorbike taxis, and the riders pull away.
Her screen reads C A B B. She stops dead on the empty platform.
Commuters hurry past her legs. Bank is gone, so she keeps sending alone, a tear running down her face.
A scuffle, and her backpack is on the floor with the suited man over it. She swallows and faces him.
A staff member tells her what is coming. Another Thai candidate has already admitted carrying a phone in. Her score is gone, and at worst she sits the exam again.
Through the glass she watches Bank answer them. Whatever he gives them, her name is not in it. She turns away.
At Bangkok arrivals Pat has a party waiting: Bank is arrested, their score is banked, and she only has to sit the exam again. She has changed her mind.
Grace puts out a hand to shake on it. Lynn walks straight past both of them.
Her father walks up at the terminal doors and asks where her boyfriend is - he wants the boy over for dinner.
He pulls her into a hug and she breaks, sobbing on his shoulder - everything she has carried since Sydney, out at once.
The party she is not at: balloons, confetti, and matching shirts printed with the score they bought. STIC 1460.
A message from Pat: Bank has already drawn his million and her share is waiting. Lynn left the chat.
A scholarship banner with Bank's face goes up on a school wall; inside, he is head-down at a desk.
The laundry has been rebuilt - new machines still in bubble wrap, a new sign over the door. Mister Bank.
A door opens onto the back workshop. Bank waits against a bench and tells her to come in. She stays put.
He called her for a reason: has she applied for GAT/PAT, because he has a job he wants her on.
He holds out a yellow leaflet: the national exam, every school in the country on the same day. She asks how much he needs.
It is not about enough, he says, but about what he can do from here. A million this time, and getting caught would not mean jail.
She says no. He turns square to her: refuse, and he will see her cut off from the exam that sends her abroad.
And not just her - Grace, Pat and every client who sat it. Her hand is on the door handle. She stops.
One more thing, he says. Her father would be very sad. Her eyes shut, then open flat.
In a white corridor her father sits beside her, head bowed. She turns away, close to tears.
He lifts his head and gives her a small smile, two chairs at the end of an empty corridor.
They walk her past the suits to a camcorder on a tripod.
She sits down across the white table and tells them everything. Bank's threat still stands; she chooses this anyway - and it costs her the exam, the money and him.
